references.text: Levi (Matthew) was also a tax collector whom Jesus called to himself. Zacchaeus shares this background as a tax collector, a profession despised in Israel ([ref:Luk 5:27|Luke 5:27]).

The rich man in the preceding story was sorrowful because he was very wealthy. Zacchaeus is also described as rich (πλούσιος), but his response to meeting Jesus becomes a contrast ([ref:Luk 18:23|Luke 18:23]).
Jesus said it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. Zacchaeus, who was rich, shows that what is impossible for people is possible for God ([ref:Luk 18:24-25|Luke 18:24-25]).

Matthew (Levi) was a tax collector when Jesus called him. Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector, meaning a leader among the tax collectors, and his meeting with Jesus follows a similar pattern ([ref:Matt 9:9|Matthew 9:9]).
Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners, which caused offense. Also in the story of Zacchaeus, people complained that Jesus went into the house of a sinful man ([ref:Matt 9:10-11|Matthew 9:10-11]).
Tax collectors and sinners stayed close to Jesus to hear him. Zacchaeus as a chief tax collector is a concrete example of this pattern ([ref:Luk 15:1-2|Luke 15:1-2]).
Tax collectors came to John to be baptized and asked what they should do. Zacchaeus's profession as a chief tax collector links him to this group seeking repentance ([ref:Luk 3:12-13|Luke 3:12-13]).
Jesus was called "the friend of tax collectors and sinners". The meeting with Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, confirms this description ([ref:Luk 7:34|Luke 7:34]).
The people's reaction shows that Zacchaeus was regarded as a sinner precisely because he was a chief tax collector. His wealth and profession made him despised ([ref:Luk 19:7|Luke 19:7]).
This is a direct continuation of the event in verse 2; the same verse describes Zacchaeus's response to Jesus's visit and his decision to give away his wealth.
